Granny Runs Geneva

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
85 year-old world record holder Deirdre Larkin takes on the Geneva Half Marathon

Unique Selling Point:
After seeing our story on active ageing, sponsors rushed forward to get world record breaker Deirdre Larkin to an overseas race.

Summary:
We go to the IAAF gold race, the Geneva Half Marathon with world champion Deirdre Larkin. At 85 years-old, this is the first race that she has run in Europe. We introduce her to the other star of our story, the world's fittest pensioner: 97 year-old world champion sprinter, Charles Eugster

Press Release:


Granny runs Geneva
At 85, Deirdre Larkin has proven that age is just a number. She holds the half-marathon world record for women over eighty-five, and she’s also broken the South African
10km record for women over 70. After seeing her story on Carte Blanche, sponsors rushed to help Deidre run her first race in Europe. Now, she’s collected another title at
the Geneva Half Marathon. Carte Blanche heads to Switzerland with this remarkable athlete

Script:


GRANNY RUNS GENEVA

V/O: Earlier this year we introduced you to Deirdre Larkin, an 85-year-old piano teacher from Randburg. After an osteoporosis scare she started running at the age of 78, and just got faster and better.

Sound up: So much better that within four years she’d broken the South African 10km record for women over 70 in a time of 54 minutes and 17 seconds.

Deirdre: Don’t know where to put them so I’m using coat hangers for the rest of the medals.

Derek: Oh, so this is the overflow rack, hey?

V/O: When we filmed her running a half marathon in Pretoria, she ran faster than ever before.

Sound up: Not only did she run her personal best she broke the world record for women 85 years and older. She finished in 2 hours, 12 minutes and 45 seconds, smashing the previous world record by over 20 minutes.

Derek: Would you like to compete in a half marathon overseas, maybe in London?

Deirdre: Oh, I’d love to, yes I’d love to somewhere or other. But it’s too expensive. As it is I’m living very comfortably because I’ve got a job. If I didn’t have a job I wouldn’t be able to do the races. I couldn’t afford all the petrol and clothes and the stuff.

V/O: And that was just the excuse M-Net, SuperSport and Multichoice needed to come to the party.

Derek: Deirdre’s pushing the trolley. I think she’s fit enough.

V/O: Last weekend Deirdre flew to Europe to participate in her first overseas competition - the magnificent Geneva Half Marathon in Switzerland.

Deirdre: I didn’t believe it. I didn’t believe it – there are so many young people who are brilliant runners – why should they take an old fogey like me?

V/O: This picturesque city ranks as one of the most expensive in the world, but also one of the cleanest. The air is fresh, the people are friendly and the race is one of the fastest in Europe. Over 50% of the runners achieve personal bests on this uniquely beautiful course.

Benjamin: The first part is in the countryside, and then the second part is in the city center, along the Lake with the finish on the famous Mont Blanc bridge, just in front of the Jet D’eau, the Geneva fountain. So, a beautiful route.

V/O: Benjamin Chandelier is the Race Director.

Derek: Do you have a lot of international visitors?

Benjamin: We have 130 different nationalities represented, of all races, so yeah. We have fun races for everyone – from 6 to 90 – so it’s a fun weekend; Three days of events here in Geneva.

Derek: How do you feel about Deirdre running the half-marathon at the age of 85?

Benjamin: It’s an honor for us to have a worldwide champion here in Geneva, so I hope she will break her personal record, which is 2 hours and 12 minutes. So, we are here to hope and congratulate her at the finish line.

V/O: With over 17 000 participants, the Race Village was pumping. The organizers sponsored Deirdre’s entry, so first stop was to collect her bib and goody bag. She was put in the 60+ category, competing against 45 other women.

Derek: How does that feel? (Derek laughs)

V/O: The expo showed the latest in running gear and technology, but then it was time for some fun.

Derek: That’s a little bit embarrassing, we’ve been chucked off the train.

Sfx:

V/O: But not quite as embarrassing as this.

Derek: The next news is we want you to run in this outfit tomorrow.

Deirdre: Hah!

Derek: Wow, look at that!

Deirdre: Come on, come on!

V/O: And can you really call it fun without a selfie?

Link: We’ve taken a break for Deirdre to charge her phone, but here in Geneva they do it the green way.

Derek: How are you enjoying Geneva so far? Beautiful city…

Deirdre: Yes, it is! But it’s all so different I don’t know what’s happening next. I’m just one state of excitement all the time.

V/O: Then it was time for a bit of sightseeing at the Palace of Nations, the home of the United Nations in Geneva. The Broken Chair is an iconic sculpture that highlights the plight of landmine victims. One of the agencies in Geneva is UNICEF - the beneficiary of the marathon.

Charlotte: This year we have big news that is really unique in the world I’m told. That’s the Extra Mile – meaning that the runners in the marathon, the semi-marathon and the relay marathon they can, after they have finished the official race – they can run another 1600m that is one mile. And with the support of Mont Blanc a donation is given to UNICEF.

Derek: Charlotte Schweizer is the spokesperson for the Children’s Fund.

Derek: Is there a specific project in mind to use that money?

Charlotte: We know that 16 000 children die every day from preventable causes, so the money collected from the Geneva marathon is used to install water pumps to provide drinking water. With the donations that we received we’ve already been able to install 465 pumps which really help giving clean water to whole villages, health centers and schools.

V/O: Race day dawned with a cold drizzle. We caught an early tram to get Deirdre out to the Start, scheduled for 8.30.

Derek: What is your goal for today?

Deirdre: Just to get to the end.

Derek: Just to finish?

Deirdre: Yes.

Derek: Not going for records?

Deirdre: Yes, I don’t think so in this rain, I’ve got to be careful of slipping.

V/O: Having fortified herself en-route with her favourite beverage - a hot cappuccino - Deirdre lined up at the Start in her usual club vest. Dwarfed by the other runners, she remained undaunted and joined in the warm-up exercises.

Sfx: French warm-up guy

V/O: At exactly 8:30 the race kicked off, with 6000 runners streaming over the line. Within 30 seconds a man slipped and fell, almost knocking Deirdre off her feet. She only just managed to dodge him and keep going.

Deirdre: I thought no, no, I’m not here to look at tumbled down people, I must keep going. So, I concentrated very hard for the next 5 minutes.

Link: Well that’s it, Deirdre’s on her way in the cold and wet, surrounded by burly male runners. But she seems to have got off alright, and we’ll be following her on the route.

Deirdre: After about 3 or 4k’s you come to the fields, and those stretch and are flat, very flat farmlands. And then up in front of you is a hill with a beautiful chapel on it. I thought I won’t have to talk at all, but I was amazed! People thumped me on the shoulders, I had to shake hands, and they said magnifique! I’d say over a hundred people spoke to me, and off they ran and left me behind.

V/O: While Deirdre was making friends in the farmlands, we had to dash back to the city and try and catch her as she came past.

Link: The sun’s come out; our camera man is following Deirdre from the back of a motorbike; we’d feel helpless here at the Finish if it wasn’t for this live tracking app: and what it says is that Deirdre should finish at 10:35 which would give her a time of 2 hours and 5 minutes – a new world record.

V/O: But we were standing at the 17k mark, which meant she had another 4 to go.

Derek: Here she is! Deirdre keep going! Deirdre! She is just incredible, I can’t believe…still smiling.

V/O: Her average pace was just under 6 minutes per km; but could she keep it up for the full 21.1km?

Deirdre: The streets were very, very narrow and we twisted and we turned. Somewhere along the line it said 1km, and I pushed it as hard as I could for the kilometer.

Derek: She’s been on the road now for exactly 2 hours. Apparently, she’s just 1 kilometer away, so a new record is definitely on the cards.

Deirdre: I looked at the watch when I came in and I saw the thing saying 2 hours 5, and I thought that’s rubbish. Then I looked at my watch and I thought ooh, maybe it’s possible?

V/O: Deirdre didn’t just break her own world record – she bettered it by 7 minutes and 24 seconds.

Derek: That’s just one of the most incredible athletic achievements I’ve ever seen. Eighty-five: two hours and five minutes, thrashing runners a quarter of her age. It’s like, well it’s like a Wayde van Niekerk event – absolutely stunning.

V/O: We rushed to congratulate her, but had to wait in line.

Italian 1: I think everybody should run like her and believe in yourself.

Italian 2: You are really an inspiration for the older generation.

Zimbo: Mandela would be proud of you.

Derek: We have a new celebrity in Geneva hey?

Deirdre: It’s lovely meeting all these different nationalities. You don’t know which country you are speaking to, or who you are speaking to – its lovely.

Derek: But it seems the older you get, the faster you get?

Deirdre: Not according to scientists, your muscle depletes.

Derek: But you break the laws of science?

Deirdre: Oh, it’s nice to break laws. I did at school.

Derek: Would you like to do another big overseas half marathon?

Deirdre: Oh, yes please! What you Say?
